_meta.description: The cohort clock — the master time axis for the whole dashboard. Age-band definitions, the spending shape within each band, and which limbs each band pays. The population and spending SERIES themselves live in reference.json, pulled from Census and BLS by scripts/fetch_reference.py; this file holds the reading of them.
_meta.source_note: Population is US Census Bureau 2023 National Population Projections, main series, Table 3 (released November 2023; 2022 is the base estimate). Spending is BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024, by age of reference person. Both refresh from primary sources weekly — see data/reference.json for the live series and retrieval dates.
_meta.revision_note: Superseded the v1 estimates on 2026-08-07. Two claims did not survive sourcing and are corrected below: the go-go band plateaus rather than declines steeply, and go-go spending is far lower relative to working life than the v1 text asserted. Both corrections are recorded in the 'corrections' block rather than quietly overwritten.

now.headline: Median boomer is 71. The cohort's centre of mass is crossing out of go-go and into slow-go.
now.body: This is the single most important sentence on the dashboard. The leading edge of the cohort turned 80 this year; the trailing edge is 62 and still working. The median sits at 71 — right at the boundary where discretionary travel and leisure spending rolls over and healthcare, home services and care spending begins its climb. The sourced data supports the direction emphatically: BLS puts average annual spending at 65–74 some 23% below the 55–64 band, with healthcare's share of the basket rising from 7.9% to 11.8% and on to 14.2% past 75.

cohort_edges.note: Now entering the band where mortality and care transitions begin to cluster. First-step wealth transfers — to surviving spouses — are happening at scale.
The largest single cohort in the wave. Sits at the top of the go-go band today; crosses into slow-go around 2032.
The centre of mass. Its position is the clock hand for the entire limb-D relay.
Still working, still accumulating, still contributing to plans. This is why limb A's flow reversal is gradual rather than a step.
Turns 65 in 2030. The pipeline behind the cohort — the reason the thesis outlives the boomer label.

bands.spend_note: Base for the index. BLS 2024: $84,946 average annual expenditure per consumer unit. Peak spending is actually the 45–54 band at $100,327 — 18% higher.
bands.label: Peak earning, still accumulating
bands.behaviour: High household income and high contribution rates. Catch-up contributions, mortgage payoff, last major durable purchases. Still net suppliers of capital to markets and net suppliers of labour.
bands.note: Gen X occupies this band for the whole thesis horizon. But the band itself shrinks from 42.1M (2022) to 38.5M (2035) before recovering — the accumulator base contracts for the next decade, which cuts against limb A sooner than the v1 text assumed.

bands.spend_note: BLS 2024: $65,354 — 23% below the 55–64 band, not 'slightly below' as v1 claimed. Transportation spend falls from $15,085 to $11,414; healthcare rises to 11.8% of the basket.
bands.label: Peak discretionary — time-rich, health-intact, asset-rich
bands.behaviour: Travel, cruises, RVs and boats, second homes, golf and leisure, restaurants, elective and quality-of-life procedures (joints, cataracts, dental, hearing). Total spending drops materially from working life, but the discretionary and experience share within a smaller basket holds up — entertainment actually rises as a share, from 4.4% at 45–54 to 4.8% here.
bands.note: The cohort's centre of mass has been sitting here. It is leaving. But see the corrections block: this band plateaus rather than collapsing, which weakens the crude version of the fade call.

bands.spend_note: BLS reports 75+ as a single bracket ($55,834) and does not split 75–84 from 85+. The index shown is the 75+ figure and applies to both this band and the next — treat the split between them as unmeasured.
bands.label: Total spend falls, mix rotates hard into care
bands.behaviour: Travel and discretionary durables drop away — transportation spend falls to $6,855, less than half the 55–64 level. Healthcare share of the basket climbs to 14.2%, roughly double the pre-retirement share. Home services and home modification replace DIY. First care decisions: in-home help, then possibly a move. Driving stops.
bands.note: The fastest-growing band on the clock through 2040, and the one the cohort is entering now. 20.3M in 2025 to 27.7M in 2035 — up 36%. This is where the thesis's demographic wind is strongest.

bands.spend_note: Inside the BLS 75+ bracket. Total spend is lower than the slow-go band and far more concentrated in medical and care, but the survey does not isolate it.
bands.label: Medical and long-term care dominate; asset release becomes forced
bands.behaviour: Spending concentrates almost entirely in medical, long-term care and housing-with-care. Care intensity rises sharply and so does its labour content. Assets are released not by choice but by care costs or by death — this is where the transfer in limb B actually executes, and where the housing stock in limb H is finally released.
bands.note: The compounding band: 7.0M (2025) to 13.7M (2040) to 17.4M (2050) — up 96% by 2040 and 149% by 2050. The most labour-intensive band to serve, which is where limb C and limb D collide directly.

projection_ref.note: The chart reads its series from reference.json so the clock cannot drift from the Census vintage behind it.

reading.body: Slow-go (75–84) grows 36% between 2025 and 2035 — 20.3M to 27.7M. The 85+ band grows 96% between 2025 and 2040 and 149% by 2050, reaching 17.4M. Against that, the go-go band peaks in 2030 at 38.0M. The demographic wind is emphatically behind the two oldest bands, and it is not behind the youngest retired one.

reading.tag: But the fade is a plateau, not a cliff
reading.body: This is the correction that matters most. Census has go-go at 38.0M in 2030, 36.9M in 2035, 35.1M in 2040 and back to 37.0M by 2050 — a drift of about 8% off the peak, then a recovery as Gen X arrives. The v1 text implied the customer base for cruise, RV and active-adult shrinks meaningfully. It does not. What actually happens is that it stops growing while those businesses are priced for growth. That is still a real and tradable divergence, but it is a relative call against a compounding care trade, not an absolute decline. Any short framed on a collapsing customer base is wrong.

The 55–64 band falls from 42.1M (2022) to 38.5M (2035) before recovering to 44.7M by 2050. v1 had this band rising throughout. The contraction arrives before the recovery, which means limb A's flow headwind — fewer contributors funding the products that depend on continuous contribution — bites in the next decade rather than the one after.

Care hours consumed scale with the 85+ band, not with the 65+ total. That band roughly doubles by 2040 against a care workforce whose training pipeline is capacity-constrained — AACN counted 93,000 qualified nursing applications turned away in 2025 alone. That is the arithmetic behind limb C, and the margin problem inside limb D.
57.8M (2022) to 71.2M (2030) to 82.2M (2050). The aggregate is the number everyone quotes; the composition inside it is the only part that is tradable.

corrections.claim: Go-go band peaks around 2030 and then declines
corrections.v1: Implied a meaningful decline in the customer base for experience-economy and active-adult businesses.
corrections.sourced: Census 2023 projections: 38.0M (2030) → 36.9M (2035) → 35.1M (2040) → 37.0M (2050). About 8% off peak, then recovery.
corrections.effect: Weakens the fade call from 'the customer disappears' to 'the customer stops growing while the price assumes otherwise'. Still a relative-value trade against the care book; no longer an argument for an outright short.

corrections.claim: Go-go spending total is only slightly below working life
corrections.sourced: BLS CEX 2024: $65,354 versus $84,946 — an index of 77, not 93.
corrections.effect: The spending drop at retirement is much sharper than v1 assumed. Strengthens the rotation argument (the basket shrinks and re-weights simultaneously) and weakens any thesis that leans on aggregate retiree spending holding up.

corrections.claim: Pre-retirement band rises through the horizon
corrections.effect: Limb A's contribution-flow headwind arrives earlier than assumed. Raises conviction in the negative case (TROW as the control variable) and in the annuity-origination trade capturing a transition from a shrinking pool.

relay.n: The go-go band peaks at 38.0M and then plateaus
relay.beneficiaries: Cruise, travel, RV/marine, active-adult housing, elective ortho and ophthalmic, golf and leisure
relay.stance: Harvest, don't short. The population supporting these businesses stops growing rather than shrinking — the trade is against a growth multiple, not against the customer.

relay.n: The slow-go band takes the growth baton — up 36%
relay.beneficiaries: Home health, chronic care management, sensory (hearing/vision), cardiology and structural heart, mobility, home modification, LTC pharmacy, Medicare Advantage
relay.stance: Accumulate. This is the core of the book and the demographic wind is strongest here.

relay.n: The 85+ band compounds fastest — up 149% by 2050
relay.beneficiaries: Skilled nursing, memory care, hospice, senior housing with care, death care, estate and trust services, the transfer itself
relay.stance: Build early where valuation allows — the demand is arithmetic, the constraint is labour and reimbursement, so own the ones that survive both.

wealth_split.note: The cohort is not one customer. Fed Distributional Financial Accounts (2026:Q1) put the boomer generation at 51.6% of US household net worth and 53.9% of corporate equities and mutual fund shares; households aged 55+ hold 73.9% of net worth. But Cerulli finds more than half of all projected transfer volume comes from the 2% of households that are HNW or UHNW — concentration within the cohort is severe, and a single 'the retiree' framing produces wrong positions for one of the two customers below.
wealth_split.boomer_share_trend: Boomer net worth share peaked at 57.6% in 2016:Q3 and has drifted to 51.6% by 2026:Q1. The transfer is not prospective — it is already visible in the data.

segments.share_note: Holds the large majority of cohort net worth; Cerulli attributes $62T of $124T in projected transfers to the top 2% of households
segments.problem: Estate and tax efficiency, not income adequacy. Will not decumulate meaningfully — dies holding.
segments.serves: Trust and estate services, private banking, alternatives access, luxury and legacy spending, philanthropy infrastructure

segments.share_note: Materially under-saved relative to a full-length retirement; US median household net worth is roughly $193k against nursing home costs near $120k a year
segments.problem: Income adequacy and out-of-pocket care cost. Will decumulate, will rely on Social Security and Medicare, and is directly exposed to limb E policy risk — the OASI trust fund depletes in 2032 with 78% of scheduled benefits payable thereafter absent legislation.
segments.serves: Annuities and guaranteed income, Medicare Advantage, value retail and dollar stores, generic pharmacy, reverse mortgage, subsidised and middle-market senior housing
